text: Hope arrives as a woman the protagonist happens to meet, which is either the oldest arrangement in the form or a fair account of how these things go. Jean-Marc Vallée has 101 minutes and a man in an expensive job coming apart inside them — an investment banker called emotionally desperate, a phrase that covers a great deal of ground and commits to none of it. The film's answer to that vagueness looks like motion: keep the man doing things, and let the comedy come from the distance between what he does and what someone in his position is supposed to do. Rotterdam's audience voted it their award, which says something real about how it lands in a full room. Widely seen and lightly held, it is the kind of film recommended more often than it is defended.

Two fourteen-year-olds, each with a home that hurts them, become the only arrangement the other has. A Japanese film released in 2012 did not need to invent its rubble, and Sion Sono sets his two classmates down in a landscape where collapse is already general — which changes what a bruise means, and what a house is worth. Crime and thriller share the billing with drama, so the tenderness between them will not be left in peace. Two hours and ten minutes is a long time to spend with children who have no adult worth appealing to, and the length is doing work: the exhaustion has to be earned in front of the camera rather than announced. What sustains them is small and practical — food, shelter, a place to sleep — and the film is exact about how little of it there is.

The device is a rewrite function, and the film uses it the way a compulsive person would: again, and again, and each time the damage lands somewhere new. A young man recovers blacked-out stretches of his childhood, discovers he can re-enter that child's body and alter what happened there, and so the film has to construct its world several times over inside 113 minutes and make every version legible at speed. Science fiction supplies the mechanism. The thriller billing is where the pressure actually sits, because the material being revised is childhood harm and the revisions keep coming down on other people. Its audience has always been far larger than its critical following, which tends to set a reputation early and leave it there. The premise survives anyway: everyone keeps a scene they would go back and edit.

A love hotel is a workplace before it is anything else, and Ryuichi Hiroki gives both shifts their 135 minutes. Guests arrive in pairs, with reasons. Staff arrive on schedule, change the sheets, mind the desk, and go home to lives of their own. Crossing those two clocks is the design: the couples believe their hours are private, while the employees know precisely how many rooms are occupied and by whom. That overlap is where the comedy comes from — nothing punctures a private drama faster than a stranger who has already processed four of them today. Tokyo's red-light district supplies the address, though the film's attention looks domestic rather than lurid: who is paying for what, who is lying about their job, which of these people will still be inside the building at dawn.

Bruno makes a rule and does not tell the woman it applies to: the next time she is late, it is over. Twenty-nine minutes is the right size for that, since the film has to run on the same fuel as its hero — time passing, someone not arriving in it. François Ozon calls it drama and romance, and the pairing is exact, because an ultimatum is only romantic while it stays secret and only dramatic once the clock starts. Waiting is not inherently tense. It becomes tense when the person waiting has decided something in advance and told no one. What she does not know cannot be negotiated with, which puts her in the odd position of failing a test she was never set. The whole short rests there: a private deadline, and the preference for being proved right over being met.

Twenty-five minutes of Berlin with the people subtracted. Chongyan Liu's documentary works through rooms and streets that have been vacated, and the vacancy is the method rather than the subject: with no one in frame to watch, attention falls onto surfaces, light, the depth of a doorway, whatever a space keeps once its occupants are gone. That puts unusual weight on sound and on the order of the shots, which are the only instruments left to argue with. The film describes its vantage as that of the departed — a large claim for a short work, and a workable one, since a camera belonging to nobody living can enter anywhere and owes no explanation. What it circles is one person's injury. The city is where it goes looking, building by building, and the looking is not neutral.

Kika does faces for a living, and this job is a corpse. She is hired to make a young man presentable for his own funeral; he sits up instead, she falls for him, and the man who hired her — Nicholas, an American author, the dead son's father — decides he wants her himself. Almodóvar files this as comedy and drama, in that order, and the order is a warning: the cruelties arrive at farce speed and are not softened by it. What holds the thing steady is craft in the literal sense, a woman who knows exactly how much colour a face will take, working in a household where everyone is composing a version of themselves for somebody else to look at. A story that opens on a body and moves straight to a rivalry is not planning to be gentle. 117 minutes, bright and very fast, with no interest in letting anyone grieve in peace.

Ove is fifty-nine, has been voted out of the presidency of his condominium association, and patrols the street as though the vote never happened. Then a neighbour reverses into his mailbox. That is the engine — a dent, and a pregnant woman named Parvaneh who declines to take the hint — while the Swedish terraced row where nobody can avoid anybody is the whole map. Among the film's honours is an Academy Award for makeup and hairstyling, an odd line to find on a comedy about bylaws and a fair clue to how much of the part is carried in a face. 116 minutes, comedy and drama in equal measure, and the machinery is made entirely of small administrative grievances: a mailbox, a rulebook, a man who has read the regulations and expects everyone else to have done the same.

For a month nobody comes, and Sachie opens the diner on a quiet Helsinki street every morning anyway. She makes rice balls, wipes the counter, waits; the film begins where most restaurant stories would already have closed the shutters. Then a first customer. Then Midori, a gangly Japanese tourist, invited to stay almost on sight. That is the rate of incident, and Naoko Ogigami holds it for 102 minutes without apologising for it. The funny parts are matters of scale: the gap between a Japanese counter routine and a Finnish street, the seriousness with which a rice ball is assembled for a customer who may not exist. What accumulates instead of plot is competence — somebody keeps the hours, keeps the place clean, keeps cooking — and eventually the street notices what has been sitting there all along.

Saori takes the work because she needs money, and the dying man in the house happens to be her father. He left her and her mother years ago and built, afterwards, a nursing home for gay men — a house of people who have arranged their own late care. So she commutes to it. The method is not a reconciliation scene but a rota: 130 minutes of shifts, meals, medication, and residents with firm opinions of their own. Haruhiko, her father's young lover, is the one who came to fetch her, which leaves him somewhere between messenger and rival. Billed as drama with no comic cover, the film takes the household seriously as a household — who cooks, who is ill, who is owed an apology, and whether an apology is even the currency in question.
